common_name: Jeepers Creepers Tiarella (Deeply Cut Maroon-Centered Foamflower)

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring or early fall once soil is workable, setting crowns level with the surrounding soil.

directions: Set divisions into humus-rich, evenly moist soil in spring or fall, spacing plants far enough apart to let their slow-creeping stolons knit together into a solid mat over a season or two. Keep the planting mulched with leaf mold to hold moisture and suppress weeds while the shallow roots establish. The deeply lobed leaves emerge green with a bold maroon-black central star that intensifies in cooler weather, and airy spikes of small white star-shaped flowers rise above the foliage in mid-spring. It makes an excellent evergreen-in-mild-climates edging or woodland groundcover beneath deciduous shade trees.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring or early fall once soil is workable, setting crowns level with the surrounding soil.

directions: Tuck divisions into moist, well-drained woodland soil enriched with compost, and water regularly the first season while the spreading stolons take hold. Once established it tolerates the dry shade at the base of trees better than many foamflowers as long as it isn't left to dry out for extended periods. Its narrow, finger-like leaf lobes radiate outward like a painted hand and darken to deep burgundy along the veins in fall and winter, complementing the fluffy white-pink spring flower spikes. The fine-textured foliage contrasts nicely with bolder hostas and ferns in a shaded border.

common_name: Excalibur Pulmonaria (Silver-Leaf Lungwort with Narrow Green Edge)

planting.note: Divide and transplant in early spring or right after flowering, planting crowns at the same depth they were growing previously.

directions: Plant in cool, humus-rich soil that stays consistently moist, choosing a site sheltered from harsh afternoon sun that can scorch the silvered leaves. Mulch to keep roots cool and shear back tattered foliage after flowering to encourage a fresh, cleaner-looking rosette for the rest of the season. The lance-shaped leaves are almost entirely silver with just a thin green margin, giving it one of the brightest foliage displays in the genus, while clusters of funnel-shaped flowers open pink and mature to blue in early spring. It brightens dim corners of the shade garden nearly year-round and pairs well with hostas and ferns.

common_name: Sissinghurst White Pulmonaria (Classic Spotted-Leaf White Lungwort)

planting.note: Divide and transplant in early spring or right after flowering, planting crowns at the same depth they were growing previously.

directions: Set plants into cool, evenly moist soil enriched with leaf mold, watering deeply during dry spells since the bristly foliage wilts quickly if it dries out. Cut back ragged summer leaves to the crown to prompt a fresh flush of clean, well-marked foliage. This heirloom selection carries the species' classic silver-spotted green leaves along with pure white, bell-shaped spring flowers that stand out against the dark foliage of neighboring hellebores and epimediums. It is an old cottage-garden favorite for lighting up shaded borders before most other perennials have leafed out.

planting.note: Divide and replant clumps in early spring while dormant, keeping the fleshy roots shallow and well spread in humus-rich soil.

directions: Plant in loose, well-drained soil generously amended with compost, sited where the finely cut foliage will get morning sun and afternoon shade. Unlike old-fashioned bleeding hearts, this hybrid keeps its handsome blue-green, fern-like leaves looking fresh through summer instead of going dormant, and it deadheads and rebounds quickly with light watering during dry stretches. Slender arching stems carry cherry-red, heart-shaped flowers from spring well into fall in cooler climates, giving far longer bloom than the species types. It combines beautifully with hostas, ferns, and heucheras as a long-season anchor for the shade border.

common_name: King of Hearts Bleeding Heart (Compact Reblooming Dicentra)

planting.note: Divide and replant clumps in early spring while dormant, keeping the fleshy roots shallow and well spread in humus-rich soil.

directions: Grow in rich, consistently moist but well-drained soil, tucking plants into rock gardens, shaded troughs, or the front of a woodland border where their compact size can be appreciated up close. Water during dry spells and avoid heavy summer humidity pockets, since good air movement helps the mounded foliage stay tidy. A hybrid of the eastern and western native fringed bleeding hearts, it forms a tight dome of ferny, blue-gray leaves topped by rosy-pink, heart-shaped flowers that reappear in flushes from spring through summer. Its small stature makes it useful for edging shaded paths where larger bleeding hearts would overwhelm the space.

common_name: Alba White Bleeding Heart (Pure White Old-Fashioned Bleeding Heart)

planting.note: Divide and replant dormant crowns in early spring or fall, handling the brittle roots carefully and setting them just below the soil surface.

directions: Plant in cool, fertile, humus-rich soil that drains well but never fully dries out, choosing a site with dappled morning light and shelter from hot afternoon sun. Expect the lush, chartreuse-green foliage and arching flower stems to die back and go fully dormant by midsummer, so mark its location and interplant with later-emerging perennials to fill the gap. Rows of pure white, heart-shaped flowers dangle from gracefully arching stems in mid-spring, offering a crisper alternative to the classic pink-and-white species. It remains a dependable, long-lived focal point for shaded borders and woodland gardens despite its brief above-ground season.

common_name: Winter Moonbeam Hellebore (Silver-Veined Early-Blooming Hybrid Hellebore)

planting.note: Transplant container-grown plants in fall or early spring into humus-rich, neutral-to-alkaline soil, disturbing the roots as little as possible.

directions: Plant in well-drained but moisture-retentive soil enriched with compost, ideally beneath deciduous shrubs or trees that provide summer shade and winter light. Established clumps need little care beyond an annual topdressing of compost and removal of old, tattered leaves in late winter to showcase the emerging flowers. This hybrid between Helleborus niger and H. sternii forms leathery, silver-veined evergreen foliage and produces abundant clusters of pink-blushed white flowers from midwinter into early spring, well ahead of most other hellebores. Its combination of ornamental foliage and extra-early bloom makes it a standout for a winter shade garden.

common_name: Hillside Black Beauty Bugbane (Dark Purple-Black Foliage Snakeroot)

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery stock in spring into deep, fertile, consistently moist soil, and stake tall flower spikes in exposed sites.

directions: Grow in rich, humus-laden soil that never dries out, since this large woodland perennial suffers quickly in drought or exposed, windy sites. Give it plenty of room at the back of the border and stake the tall bottlebrush flower spikes if the planting site is breezy. The deeply cut foliage emerges near-black and holds its dark purple color through the season better than many older bugbane cultivars, contrasting dramatically with the fragrant white flower spikes that open in late summer and early fall. Bees are drawn to the late-season blooms, and the dark foliage makes an excellent backdrop for lighter-colored shade perennials in front of it.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery stock in spring into deep, fertile, consistently moist soil, and stake tall flower spikes in exposed sites.

directions: Site in cool, evenly moist, humus-rich soil with protection from midday sun and wind, mulching to keep the shallow root system from drying out over summer. Established clumps are long-lived and rarely need division, though a yearly compost topdressing keeps growth vigorous. Fresh green, finely divided foliage forms a tidy mound topped in late summer by branching, slightly arching spikes of small white flowers with a light, sweet fragrance that draws late-season pollinators. It extends the bloom season in the shade garden well past most perennials and works nicely massed at the back of a woodland border.
